newsitem.title: UK: LME copper hesitates after hitting fresh highs.
newsitem.headline: LME copper hesitates after hitting fresh highs.

text.p: LME copper extended its rally on Tuesday afternoon, but ran into forward selling and profit taking after notching up fresh highs.
Many of the other metals marked time, while tin dived after failing to sustain higher numbers.

Three months copper skipped to $2,433 per tonne in inter-office trade after hectic activity on the morning kerb, the highest since early March. Widespread buying was seen, including by funds, traders said.
But once ring trading resumed in the afternoon, producer selling and profit-taking eroded the gains, and prices ended the afternoon kerb only $8 higher at $2,417.
"Fundamentally it still looks good, but I think it may need to build a base above $2,400," said analyst Helen Williamson of broker Brandeis.
The next major target is $2,440, the high of March 7.
The premium of cash over three months metal was slightly narrower at $53/$56 compared to $60/$65 on Monday.

Tight supplies were accented by a report from the International Copper Study Group that said world copper consumption for January and February 1997 was 7.5 percent higher than the same period a year earlier.
Aluminium continued to move sideways after last week's gains, ending the day unchanged at $1,670.
The market may need further consolidation or even a correction before it can gather enough steam to mount a raid on March highs just above $1,700, analysts said.
Tin lost heart after failing to sustain gains from last week's rally and ended with charts looking shaky again.
Prices broke below the 100-day moving average at $5,868 as well as short-term 10 and 30-day averages.
But Williamson said the market was merely range-trading within a wide band between the April 11 low of $5,600 and Friday's $5,920 high.
Last business in nickel was also weaker, but not to the extent in tin, finishing down $65 at $7,770.

Norilsk Nickel confirmed traders reports on Tuesday that exports are being delayed by flooding at Russia's Arctic port of Dudinka, but this is a seasonal occurrence and was shrugged off by the market.
Analysts are generally bullish for nickel, but one said that stainless steel firms have delayed price hikes, which may indicate they are concerned stocks are building up.
Broker Waterside Futures said the market reached an overbought situation on its move to $7,900 on Monday and a correction is likely to take it down to around $7,640.
"Nickel has a habit of under-correcting in the short-term, however, so such a move may not materialise," the broker's WaveTrack report said.
Once prices surmount the March 4 $8,330 peak, no major resistance is expected until $10,000 it added.
Lead was moribund, trapped in a narrow range, ending the day $8 softer at $622.
Zinc moved sideways again after last week's sharp move higher, finishing $2 firmer at $1,337.
Alloy ended at $1,523/27, little changed from Monday's $1,520/30.
--Eric Onstad, London Newsroom +44 171 542-8065
